content.comment_body: Hello forum members, I've enjoyed working with [product_name] modules on many projects, but the logic behind the firmware versioning still confuses me. For example, why does version 1.81.03 correspond to FS:06, while 1.82.02 matches FS:02? Why does a higher version number sometimes have a lower FS:0x designation? What do the letters 'FS' represent? Could someone clarify the relationship between [product_name] basis module version, [product_name] programming software version, firmware version, and FS:0x status? Apologies for my English. Thanks!

Welcome! FS is the German abbreviation for production status (Fertigungsstand). Regarding program downloads to your new [product_name], usually a new series starts with production status FS01. For instance, the first generation of [product_name] basis modules had the identifier FS01-FS03, with firmware versions between V1.08.01 and V1.08.03 (updates weren’t possible). The programming software version used was V8.0. Later, in October 2016, the second generation appeared – same order numbers, but hardware identified as FS4, with software version V8.1, and production statuses FS04-FS06. This was a break from previous numbering logic. Firmware updates became possible from then on. The most recent release changed order numbers and reset production status numbers (FS01, FS02) for versions 1.82.01 and 1.82.02, and software version V8.2 (and V8.2.1). Security firmware updates are now available for recent generations due to vulnerabilities. The next major version is scheduled for release in October 2020.

Thank you for your thorough explanation! I doubt even the official training staff could explain it better. Sometimes [company_name] makes things a bit confusing, but their products remain my preferred choice for all my projects. Best regards from Brazil.

For those using older [product_name] standard modules identified with FS01 (firmware v1.08.01), there’s no way to protect against certain vulnerabilities: CVE-2019-10919 (missing authentication, allowing reconfiguration and project file access), CVE-2019-10920 (use of hard-coded encryption keys), and CVE-2019-10921 (passwords stored in cleartext). Source: [url]
Could you share any new details or updates related to your previous post?
Just wanted to highlight that older devices remain vulnerable, and this forum can serve as a useful reference. Hope someone has an up-to-date help file summarizing [product_name] versioning.
That doesn't answer my earlier question. What new information do you have? As mentioned before, older [product_name] modules can't be updated (see the attached file above in my earlier post).
My intention was simply to notify about the CVEs.
How does this relate to the actual topic: firmware versioning logic (FS:0x)?

It doesn't. Also, the original topic relates more to hardware than just software. This discussion could go on indefinitely, but sharing this here may help inform other FS01-FS03 users. Appreciated the explanation of [company_name] product nomenclature and upgradability.
If you meant to discuss something else, please post in a more appropriate topic. Start a new thread for that.

analysis.insight_summary: Users are seeking clarity on how firmware versions correspond to production status codes (FS:0x) for [company_name] modular devices, noting that revised schemes sometimes mean a newer firmware relates to a lower FS number and these inconsistencies disrupt predictability. Detailed explanations have helped, but owners of older modules express concern they cannot update or address known security issues. There’s a recognized need for improved documentation outlining the relationships between hardware generations, firmware, and programming software, especially where security and compatibility are impacted.
analysis.user_expectations: Users want easier-to-understand and consistent versioning across firmware, hardware, and configuration tools, as well as complete documentation that explains these interrelations. They expect to be able to maintain security on all installed devices.
